history.text:
Why cortisol matters for sleep

Cortisol is the hormone that helps you wake up. It normally rises in the early morning and falls through the day, reaching its lowest point around bedtime.

When stress keeps cortisol high in the evening, the body stays alert. Many women notice this as trouble falling asleep, or waking around 3am with a busy mind.

Gentle habits that support the natural rhythm:
- Get daylight within an hour of waking.
- Keep caffeine to the morning.
- Dim lights and screens an hour before bed.
- Wind down with something calming, like a short walk or reading.

If poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks, talk with your healthcare provider.

Cortisol is the hormone that helps you wake up. It normally rises in the early morning and falls through the day, reaching its lowest point around bedtime.

When stress keeps cortisol high in the evening, the body stays alert. Many women notice this as trouble falling asleep, or waking around 3am with a busy mind. Hormonal shifts in perimenopause can make this more common.

Gentle habits that support the natural rhythm:
- Get daylight within an hour of waking.
- Keep caffeine to the morning.
- Eat a balanced dinner, not too late.
- Dim lights and screens an hour before bed.
- Wind down with something calming, like a short walk, stretching or reading.

If poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks, or you feel unwell during the day, talk with your healthcare provider.

items.title: Can I take magnesium at night?

history.text:
Can I take magnesium at night?

Many people find an evening routine helps them relax before sleep, and magnesium is a mineral often discussed for this.

Before starting any supplement, check with your healthcare provider or pharmacist, especially if you take other medicines or have kidney problems. They can tell you whether it suits you and what form is right for you.

Intermittent fasting in perimenopause

Intermittent fasting means eating within a set window of the day. Some women find it helps with energy and weight; others find it makes sleep, mood or hot flushes worse during perimenopause.

Things to keep in mind:
- Hormones are already changing, so start gently and notice how you feel.
- Eat enough protein and vegetables in your eating window.
- Stop if you feel dizzy, very tired or anxious.

If you have diabetes, a history of disordered eating, or take regular medicines, talk with your healthcare provider before trying it.
